20289-herein-is-love-a-study-of-the-bibl:
Reuel L. Howe wrote Herein Is Love, a study of the biblical doctrine of love. Howe means the book for study groups of parents and teachers. Pastors and church students will gain new insights from it, he says. Any person keen on the Christian life is also addressed directly.

Love, in the Bible, is more than feeling, Howe argues throughout. It shapes how parents, teachers, and neighbors treat one another daily. Group use matters because such love is learned in shared life. Readers get a warm, practical study of faith's central command.
20843-an-estimate-of-the-value-and-influ:
Thomas Hill Green went to Rugby at fourteen, then to Balliol College, Oxford, in 1855. There he fell under Jowett, the famed translator of Plato. Fred Newton Scott's study opens with that life before it weighs fiction's worth.

An Estimate of the Value and Influence of Works of Fiction asks what novels do to readers. Scott, a noted teacher of English, treats fiction as a real force. He weighs its sway on morals, taste, and thought. The essay shows scholars of the 1890s taking the novel with full gravity at last.
20946-memoirs-of-the-jacobites-of-1715-a:
Many Jacobites sank into oblivion, their motives dim and their sacrifices untold, says volume one. Memoirs of the Jacobites of 1715 and 1745 vows to set that record straighter. Mrs. Catherine Thomson drew these lives to rescue names from neglect.

Two failed risings for the exiled Stuarts frame the lives told here. Lords who lost heads, lands, and homes fill the first volume's pages. Letters and family lore back the tales of loyalty and loss. Readers meet the losing side of Britain's last civil wars in human terms, not as mere rebels in a victor's book.
21196-little-masterpieces-of-american-wi:
Thomas L. Masson edited this 1903 Doubleday, Page anthology of short American humour, the first of a series of little masterpieces. Washington Irving, Oliver Wendell Holmes, and Benjamin Franklin stand at its head. Mark Twain, Josh Billings, Charles Dudley Warner, and Henry Ward Beecher also appear.

Twain even supplied a handwritten note joking that his assistant compilers chose his pieces, which is why there are not more of them. Selections come from writers like S. W. Foss, James Whitcomb Riley, and Mary Mapes Dodge. The volume collects the short comic pieces, verses, and sketches that filled American magazines and newspapers of the age.
21339-the-works-of-aphra-behn-volume-i:
Montague Summers edited this first volume of Aphra Behn's collected works in 1915, with a long memoir of her mysterious life. Behn was among the first English women to earn her living by writing. The volume holds four plays: The Rover in two parts, The Dutch Lover, and The Roundheads.

The Rover follows banished cavaliers in carnival Naples, full of disguise, duels, and courtesans with hearts. The Roundheads turns to Civil War politics under the subtitle The Good Old Cause. Summers's preface warns that early claims about Behn need hard proof before belief. His edition began the modern recovery of her work for readers and stages.
21752-my-doggie-and-i:
A man and his small, shapeless, hairy dog stand at the center of this warm Ballantyne tale. The narrator insists his pet is not a dog but a doggie, a class apart in charm. Dumps, as he is called, has short legs, long hair, and a face veiled by both. Friends laugh at him, and his master does not care at all.

Ballantyne tells how the two met on a dusty country lane and what grew between them. The book is part love letter, part comic defense of an unlovely pet. It shows the gentle side of a writer known for storms and battles. Any reader who has loved an odd dog will know exactly what he means.
22018-the-son-of-monte-cristo-volume-i:
The Son of Monte-Cristo continues Alexandre Dumas's famous tale of the Count of Monte Cristo into the next generation. This first of two volumes appeared in the thirty-volume Collier edition of Dumas's works. It opens with a marriage contract that ends in ruin. A family tragedy and a strange trial follow fast.

Benedetto the murderer escapes the prison hulks, and death sentences hang over more than one head. Old friends of the Count, Cavalcanti and Danglars among them, move through the plot. Monte-Cristo himself returns before the volume closes. Readers who finished the Count's own story get the same fare here: disguise, vengeance, and last-minute rescue.
22405-the-olden-time-series-vol-2-the-da:
The Olden Time Series, volume two, recalls the days of the spinning wheel in New England, in 1885. It gathers scraps of colonial life before factories changed home work. A motto from Hazlitt frames its backward look.

Hazlitt argues that the past, having ceased to be, counts as nothing. The future, yet to come, has never been anything either. Against that cold logic, the series preserves small old facts. Spinning wheels, home cloth, and daily customs get their due. Such antiquarian books saved details that grand histories ignored. Readers interested in early American homes will find the volume a storehouse of humble, telling particulars.
22832-the-cathedral-church-of-canterbury:
Canterbury Cathedral gets a full guidebook treatment in this second edition from the Bell's Cathedrals series. The author names his authorities up front. They include Willis on the cathedral's building history and Dean Stanley's memorials of the city and church.

Inside, readers tour the building stone by stone. The guide explains the choir, chapels, tombs, and windows, and ties each feature to the bishops, kings, and pilgrims who shaped the church. Becket's shrine and murder naturally loom large in the story. Compact and earnest, the volume was made for visitors who wanted facts in hand while they walked. It still serves that purpose well.
23100-a-budget-of-paradoxes-volume-i:
Augustus De Morgan collects cranks in A Budget of Paradoxes, volume one. De Morgan flags one large omission himself. He leaves out the famous quarrel between Sir James South and Troughton over mounting the great equatorial telescope at Campden Hill. Someday, when no living astronomer remembers the feud, the omitted sketch will make fine reading, De Morgan promises, as history and character study both.

De Morgan, a mathematician, spent years answering circle-squarers, perpetual-motion men, and other paradoxers, and this book is his museum of them. The letters are funny, sad, and endlessly inventive. Astronomy feuds like the Campden Hill quarrel show that professionals could match amateurs in stubbornness. The Budget remains the classic tour of respectable delusion, guided by a wit who pitied his specimens even while refuting them.
a-selection-from-the-writings-of-guy-de-: A selection of stories by Guy de Maupassant, the French master of the short story. In tales famous for their ironic twists, he writes of peasants and prostitutes, clerks and soldiers, love and greed, always with a cold, clear eye. Maupassant could do in ten pages what other novelists needed three hundred for, and this volume shows the range of his pitiless art.
al-masudi-prairies-dor-meynard-vol-i:
Barbier de Meynard began the complete French version of the Muruj al-Dhahab of al-Masudi in 1861. His Les Prairies d'Or, the Meadows of Gold, ran to nine tomes by 1877, made with Pavet de Courteille for the Société Asiatique. This first tome opens the set. Al-Masudi, the tenth-century traveler of Baghdad, is the author.

In his opening books the author ranges over the creation, the shape of the earth, the seas, and the old kings of Persia and the east. He writes as a man who has sailed the Indian Ocean and asked questions in every port. The French text carries notes for names and places. This is the full Masudi that Sprenger's English start never finished.

freytag-pictures-of-german-life-xviiixix:
Modern Germany takes shape in the first volume of Freytag's Pictures of German Life for the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries, in English. Frederick the Great, the Napoleonic wars, and the rise of the middle class mark the road. Freytag traces change in homes and workshops as much as in ideas and battles.

Enlightenment talk in coffee houses gives way to factories, railways, and new professions. He watches manners, dress, and family life shift as the old estates loosen their grip. Lively and opinionated, the history argues that Germany became modern from the household outward. The novelist's eye for character keeps abstractions grounded in people. Readers finish with a felt sense of two centuries of daily transformation.
freytag-pictures-of-german-life-xvxvii-c:
German daily life from the 1400s through the 1600s fills the first volume of Gustav Freytag's Pictures of German Life, presented here in English. The Reformation, the peasants' wars, and the Thirty Years' War pass across these pages. Freytag tells the great events through homes, workshops, and market squares rather than battlefields alone.

Costume, craft, food, and faith receive the novelist's eye for telling detail. Ordinary people carry three crowded centuries in this telling. The volume made cultural history popular in Germany, a genre Freytag practically founded there. Rich in fact and warm in sympathy, it brings its centuries vividly to life. Historians still respect the research under the readable surface.

An FBI investigative report from the Memphis office, dated June 10, 1968, covers the hunt for Dr. Martin Luther King Jr.'s killer. Its span runs from April 4, the day King was shot in Memphis, to June 10. Two months of a national manhunt are gathered into one office's account.

Memphis was the office of origin because the crime happened on its ground. Reports like this one collected interviews, leads, and arrests into the case's spine. By June 10 the search had reached its end in an arrest abroad, and the report closes that first phase of the case.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_korea-nu:
Under President George H.W. Bush, the United States tried an opening diplomatic strategy toward North Korea. Robert A. Wampler edited this briefing book, number 610, published in November 2017. Declassified documents show Defense Secretary Dick Cheney warning allies about moving too fast toward force.

Cheney told partners that military force could jeopardize the initial diplomatic approach to Pyongyang. At the same time Washington had to keep Seoul aligned on political, diplomatic, and security interests. That balancing act, pressure beside engagement, defined Korea policy for decades. The early 1990s version is preserved here in the participants' own paper.

podcast-dannyjones-U7niXhUEC-I:
Physicist Thomas Campbell worked for NASA and defense contractors before writing a trilogy arguing that reality is a computed simulation governed by consciousness. On Danny Jones's podcast, he explains why he left the inside track. He says he discovered the truth of the universe. In his account, the physical world is information, and love is its operating principle.

Campbell presents his theory with an engineer's diagrams and a mystic's conclusions, a combination that has earned him a devoted following. Jones works through the model and its tests. The theory is Campbell's own and stands outside physics as practiced, a fact he acknowledges cheerfully. The episode preserves a credentialed insider's complete alternative cosmology, delivered with unusual serenity. Listeners can take the physics as metaphor or as claim, which is the choice Campbell himself finally offers.
podcast-tuckercarlson-mUH4Co2wE-I:

The pair take on Ozempic, birth control pills, and the food and drug giants they say shape bad health policy. They argue that chronic disease is a business model, not an accident. Carlson asks what a real fix would look like. Health-conscious viewers get two whistleblowers naming names and numbers.
t-mann-bashan-and-i:
Thomas Mann's hunting pointer Bashan inspired the most personal book he ever wrote. Bashan and I, in Herman George Scheffauer's English translation, follows the dog through Munich fields and seasons while his master watches, thinks, and delights. Part memoir and part meditation, the little book charmed readers who knew Mann only as a solemn novelist.

Through Bashan, Mann reflects on nature, loyalty, patience, and the writer's odd working life. The dog's illnesses, hunts, and daily habits receive the same care Mann gave his fictional dynasties. Tender and funny, the portrait keeps breaking into unexpected depth. It shows a great ironist relaxing into plain affection. Animal lovers and Mann readers alike claim the book as a favorite.

tieck-the-rebellion-in-the-cevennes-vol-:
Ludwig Tieck set his historical novel amid the Camisard rising in the Cevennes, and this first volume reaches English readers in translation. French Protestants, hunted under Louis XIV, take to the mountains and fight back. Faith, cruelty, and courage meet in a wild, steep land.

Tieck, a leader of German Romantic writing, sides with the rebels' plight. Young prophets, royal troops, and secret worship fill his pages. He turns a grim religious war into a tale of high feeling and peril. The opening volume sets up a neglected masterwork of German historical fiction, rich in mood and pity.
un-ga-res-united-nations-general-assembl:
Annex I to General Assembly Resolution 13, from the first session in 1946, holds the recommendations of the Technical Advisory Committee on Information. The committee began from a simple claim. The United Nations could not reach its goals unless people around the world were told, in full, what it aimed to do and what it was doing.

The annex calls for a Department of Public Information. It would be led by an Assistant Secretary-General. It would work through press, publications, radio, films, and branch offices. The annex urges open access for the press to United Nations work. It also urges support for national information services and study of public opinion. It states plainly that the department should inform and not spread propaganda.

Annex I to General Assembly Resolution 14, from 1946, holds the provisional financial regulations for the United Nations. Those rules governed United Nations money in the new organization's first year. They set the financial year as the calendar year. They deal with the provisional budget for 1946 and the first annual budget that would follow it.

Inside, the regulations create a working capital fund. The fund is built from advances by member states. The rules require contributions in the currency of the host country. They give the Secretary-General control over allotments and payments. They also set rules for accounts, bank deposits, and internal checks on spending. They cover the naming of outside auditors to review the books for 1946.
